paras: The New Bern State Guard chase of 1903 occurred on the morning of July 28, 1903, when soldiers of the Second Regiment of the North Carolina State Guard, passing through New Bern on their way home from encampment, chased a young Black boy until he fell on the railroad track and broke his leg. No one was identified or punished, and the Charlotte Observer later called such conduct "a reproach to the State Guard."

Returning from the Morehead City encampment, the regiment's trains were collected at New Bern, where some companies branched off; according to Capt. Van Dalen Stronach of Raleigh's Oak City Guards, only the men in charge of baggage were not under guard.

A dispatch from New Bern said "many soldiers got after and frightened a young negro boy of tender age," who fled and broke his leg in two places in a fall on the track; Dr. R. S. Primrose dressed the injury. Stronach, who said he watched from the ground, blamed only the baggage-detail men, who chased the youth "apparently with only fun in view" until his foot caught under the rail.

By Stronach's account, Col. Bragaw "could not give the men engaged" but had the injured youth attended and arranged for his care after the troops left. No report of an arrest or discipline appears in the coverage, and the victim is never named.

The Raleigh News & Observer ran the first report as "FRIGHTEN A LITTLE NEGRO" and two days later "WHO CHASED NEGRO?", an interview whose subheading said Stronach "Exonerates Raleigh Company." In September the Scotland Neck Commonwealth reprinted, under "Rowdy Soldiers," a Charlotte Observer passage that grouped the incident with the chasing of Black people at the Biltmore encampment and judged it "unworthy of soldiers." The same column condemned Booker Washington's party for eating in a white hotel dining room. No Black-press coverage was found.
The dispatch called the victim a boy "of tender age" chased by "many soldiers," while Stronach, an officer defending his company, said he was "grown in size" and that only the baggage men took part.

reader.title: New Bern State Guard chase of 1903
bases: A group of soldiers off duty chased a Black boy or young man, who fell and broke his leg during the chase (A1, A2); no blows, weapons or threat to kill are reported, so it is a group assault by pursuit rather than a lynching attempt.

The New Bern dispatch (A1) and Capt. Stronach's eyewitness interview (A2) agree that soldiers chased a Black youth who fell on the track and broke his leg, and the Charlotte Observer, quoted in A3, repeats the core event; they differ only on the victim's age, the number of chasers and which men were involved.

accounts.label: New Bern dispatch
accounts.gist: Many soldiers of the passing Second Regiment got after and frightened a young Black boy, who fled from their uniforms and demeanor, fell on the track and broke his leg in two places.

accounts.label: Officer's account (Capt. Stronach)
accounts.gist: Only the unguarded baggage-detail men, 'apparently with only fun in view', chased a youth 'grown in size'; his foot caught under the rail and he broke his leg near the foot, and the men ran back to the baggage car.

accounts.label: Charlotte Observer editorial
accounts.gist: Some returning troops 'set upon a negro boy' at Newbern and chased him until he fell and broke a leg, one of several acts of State Guard misconduct that summer.

framing.detail: The News & Observer's dispatch, headed 'FRIGHTEN A LITTLE NEGRO', stressed the victim's youth and fear of the uniforms without comment.
The follow-up 'WHO CHASED NEGRO?' centered on clearing the Raleigh company, gave the officer's view that the chase was in fun, and cast doubt on the victim being a boy.

Under 'Rowdy Soldiers', the Commonwealth endorsed the Charlotte Observer's view that the conduct was 'unworthy of soldiers', while the same column attacked Booker Washington and Black demands for equal service.
